tagline: Europe's youngest country, and its youngest people
overview:
Kosovo is a small landlocked territory in the central Balkans, about the size of Delaware and Rhode Island together, ringed by mountains and bordered by Albania, North Macedonia, Montenegro, and Serbia. The capital, Pristina, is a lively city of cafés, new glass buildings, and a huge library covered in domes and metal netting. Kosovo declared independence from Serbia in 2008, but its status is disputed: more than 100 countries, including the United States and most of the European Union, recognize it as a country, while Serbia, Russia, China, and others do not, and it is not a member of the United Nations.

About 1.6 million people live in Kosovo, and it has the youngest population in Europe, with roughly half under 30. Most are Albanian and Muslim; Serbs, mostly Orthodox Christian, form the largest minority, living mainly in the north and in scattered enclaves. Albanian and Serbian are the official languages. Kosovo is a parliamentary republic and uses the euro. Many families depend on money sent home by relatives working in Germany and Switzerland, and young Kosovars have become known for pop music and soccer talent.
landAndNature: Kosovo is a high basin, mostly between 400 and 700 meters above sea level, split by low hills into two plains: the Kosovo plain in the east and the Dukagjin plain in the west. Mountains rise on all sides. The Šar Mountains in the south and the Accursed Mountains in the west top 2,600 meters, with Gjeravica at 2,656 meters the highest peak, and their slopes hold ski runs at Brezovica, alpine lakes, and old beech forests. The Rugova Canyon near Peja is a deep gorge with waterfalls and caves. The Mirusha waterfalls cascade through 13 lakes. Rivers such as the Sitnica and White Drin flow to three different seas. Brown bears, wolves, lynx, and chamois live in the mountains. Winters are cold and snowy, summers warm.
peopleAndCulture: Kosovo Albanians share language and customs with Albania, including the besa code of honor and hospitality, and Serbian culture centers on the medieval Orthodox monasteries of Dečani and Gračanica, which are UNESCO World Heritage Sites. Meals begin with flija, a layered pancake baked slowly under a metal dome, or with flaky pite pastries, and include grilled meats, peppers stuffed with cheese, and ajvar, a red pepper spread. Coffee culture fills Pristina's streets with cafés. Weddings are lavish, and the traditional plis, a white felt cap, is worn by older men. Music ranges from folk songs with the çifteli lute to pop stars Dua Lipa and Rita Ora, both of Kosovar heritage. Soccer, judo, and basketball are the top sports; Majlinda Kelmendi won Kosovo's first Olympic gold in judo in 2016.
history: Illyrians and later Romans lived here, and Slavs arrived in the 600s. In the Middle Ages Kosovo was the center of the Serbian kingdom, which built its great monasteries there. The Battle of Kosovo in 1389 against the Ottomans became a founding legend of Serbian history, and the Ottoman Empire ruled for more than 500 years, during which most of the population became Albanian-speaking and Muslim. Serbia took Kosovo in 1912, and it became a province of Yugoslavia with self-rule under Tito. Serbia stripped that autonomy in 1989, and tensions grew into war in 1998 and 1999, in which thousands died and hundreds of thousands of Albanians were driven from their homes before NATO bombing forced Serbian forces out. The United Nations administered Kosovo until it declared independence on February 17, 2008.
funFacts: Kosovo has the youngest population in Europe, with an average age of about 30.
Pristina has a statue of Bill Clinton and a street named after him, thanking the United States for its role in 1999.
The National Library in Pristina, covered in 99 domes and metal mesh, is often listed among the world's strangest buildings.
Kosovo joined the Olympics in 2016 and won gold at its very first Games, in women's judo.
Pop stars Dua Lipa and Rita Ora both have Kosovar Albanian parents and are celebrated as heroes in Pristina.
